title: More Than a Look
paragraphs: The word Bauhaus now evokes a recognisable look: flat roofs, white walls, steel tubing and clean sans-serif lettering. Yet the school that Walter Gropius founded in Weimar in 1919 set out less to invent a style than to reform how designers were trained. Gropius wanted to dissolve the boundary between fine art and craft, so that artists and craftspeople would learn side by side.

Teaching was organised around workshops rather than lecture halls. Students began with a preliminary course in which they experimented with materials and form before choosing a specialism such as metalwork, weaving or furniture. After the school moved to Dessau in 1925, its workshops increasingly produced prototypes intended for industrial manufacture, a shift that brought the ideals of the founders into contact with the demands of the market.

The experiment was short-lived. The school relocated again to Berlin in 1932 under Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and closed in 1933 under pressure from the new Nazi government, which regarded it with hostility. Its teachers and students then scattered across Europe and the United States, carrying its methods into schools, firms and architectural practices abroad. In 1996 UNESCO added Bauhaus sites in Weimar and Dessau to its World Heritage List.

Popular accounts often attach the slogan 'form follows function' to the school, but the phrase is usually credited to the American architect Louis Sullivan, who used it before the Bauhaus existed. The confusion is telling. Reducing the Bauhaus to a set of visual signatures obscures what was arguably its more durable contribution: the conviction that design could be taught as a disciplined inquiry into materials, use and production.
